title: How to stop wasting time on your phone: a setup that actually sticks
description: The phone settings that make it harder to scroll on autopilot, and the one trick that stops you switching your own limits off.
intro: Most screen-time plans fail for one reason: the person setting the limit is the same person who turns it off at 11pm. This setup takes about fifteen minutes and is built around making the easy thing harder to undo.

sections.h: 1. Give the passcode to someone else
p: On an iPhone, Screen Time lets you set a separate passcode for its limits (Settings, Screen Time, Lock Screen Time Settings). Ask a partner or friend to type a code you don't know. Now an app limit actually holds, because you can't approve "ignore limit" yourself.
On Android, Digital Wellbeing app timers can be paused by you, so the same idea needs a parental-controls setup (Google Family Link) with someone else as the parent account.

sections.h: 2. Make the apps slower to reach
list: Move social apps off the home screen into the App Library or a folder on the last page.
Log out of them, so every visit starts with a password.
Delete the app and use the website version instead; it is clunkier, which is the point.
Turn off notifications for every app that isn't a person messaging you.
Try grayscale: on iPhone, Accessibility, Display & Text Size, Color Filters, Grayscale. On Android, Bedtime mode can turn the screen grey at night.
Set an app limit that starts low, like 15 minutes a day, and raise it only if it feels impossible.
Charge it outside the bedroom and use a cheap alarm clock.
Pick one place in your home where the phone lives during meals and the first hour of the morning.

sections.h: Why limits still get switched off
p: Every one of these can be undone by you in a few taps when you're tired. That is the gap Hard Lock is meant to close: a block only a friend you choose, or a tag you keep in another room, can lift, with a heads-up to them if you try to remove it.

title: Cash drawer count sheet by denomination (with the deposit worked out)
description: A copy-paste count sheet for closing a register: every bill, coin and roll, the starting float, the deposit, and over or short against your POS.
intro: Closing a drawer goes wrong in two places: adding up the coins, and working out what to take out for the deposit. This sheet does both in the same order every night, so anyone on staff can close and the numbers can be checked the next morning.

sections.h: Work out the deposit and over or short
list: Starting float: the cash the drawer started with, the same amount every day (for example $150).
Deposit = counted total minus starting float. Take that out in large bills first, so the float left behind is small bills and coins.
Expected cash = starting float + cash sales - cash refunds - cash paid out + cash paid in. Your POS shows this on the drawer or shift report.
Over or short = counted total minus expected cash. Write it down every night, even when it is zero.
The person who counts is not the person who worked the drawer, or a second person checks the count.
Count bills face up and in the same order every time; it makes recounts fast.
Keep each sheet with the deposit slip. A pattern of small shorts on the same shift is worth a conversation.

sections.h: Doing this on a phone instead of paper
p: Drawer Count is a tool being tested for Square sellers: staff type the counts on a phone or tablet, the total and deposit are worked out, the count is compared with Square’s expected cash for that shift, and every count is logged with who did it.

title: Merchant Center misrepresentation: check your feed against your product pages before you appeal
description: A step-by-step way to find the products where your feed and your live pages disagree, plus the store-wide pages reviewers look at, before you request a review.
intro: Stores suspended for "misrepresentation" keep hiring freelancers for the same job: open every product page and compare it with the feed. You can do a first pass yourself with a spreadsheet. This page shows how, and what to look at.

sections.h: 1. Get your feed into a spreadsheet
p: Download your product list from Merchant Center, or open the feed file your store or app submits. Keep these columns: id, title, link, price, sale price, availability, and shipping if you set it per product.
Sort by your best sellers or highest prices first. Those are the pages a reviewer is most likely to open.

sections.h: 2. Open each link and compare, field by field
list: Price: the price on the page matches the feed price, in the same currency, with no extra charge added only at checkout.
Sale price: if the page shows a sale, the feed has the sale price and the sale is still running.
Availability: "in stock" in the feed means the product can actually be added to the cart on the page.
Link: the link opens that exact product, not the home page, a collection, a login wall or an error.
Variants: if the feed lists a size or colour, the page opens with that variant selected or shows its price.
Structured data: if your theme adds product markup, its price and availability match what the page shows.

sections.h: 3. Check the pages every reviewer reads
list: Contact details a customer can use: an email address or phone number, and a business address if you have one.
A returns and refunds policy with the actual window and who pays return shipping.
A shipping policy whose costs and times match what checkout charges.
Terms of service and a privacy policy, linked from the footer.
Checkout over https, with the payment methods you show actually working.

sections.h: 4. Keep a record of what you fixed
p: Add a column for what you changed on each row and the date. When you request a review, you know exactly what is different from the version that was suspended.
sections.pre: id | link | feed price | page price | feed availability | page availability | fixed? | note

sections.h: Why this takes so long by hand
p: Every product is a separate page, and prices change. A store with a few hundred products means hours of opening tabs, and the check is out of date the next time prices change. That is the part Feed Match is meant to do for you, if enough stores ask for it.

title: Wedding family formals shot list template
description: A copy-paste list of family and group combinations, in the order that lets people leave as soon as theirs is done, plus the three questions to ask the couple a month out.
intro: Family formals go wrong for one reason: nobody agreed the list before the day. This is the template I use. Copy it, fill the names, send it back to the couple to approve, and give a copy to one loud relative.

sections.h: Ask the couple these three things a month before
list: Who must be in a photo, by name, including anyone elderly, unwell or with small children, so they go first.
Any two people who should not be posed together. Ask it plainly; it saves a scene.
Who is the helper: one relative or the planner who knows faces and will round people up while you shoot.

sections.h: The list, largest groups first, then peel off
sections.pre:
1. Couple + everyone (both families, whole wedding party)
2. Couple + both families together
3. Couple + Partner A's full family (parents, siblings, siblings' partners and kids, grandparents)
4. Couple + Partner A's parents and siblings
5. Couple + Partner A's parents
6. Couple + Partner A's grandparents
7. Couple + Partner B's full family
8. Couple + Partner B's parents and siblings
9. Couple + Partner B's parents
10. Couple + Partner B's grandparents
11. Couple + full wedding party
12. Partner A + their side of the party
13. Partner B + their side of the party
14. Couple + flower children and ring bearers (do this one early; they will not last)
15. Any named must-haves the couple added (godparents, chosen family, the friend who introduced them)

p: Allow about two minutes per combination with a helper calling names, three without one. Fifteen combinations is roughly half an hour, and that is before anyone wanders off to the bar.
Shoot the oldest and youngest first and release them. Shoot the largest group second while everyone is still gathered. Everything after that is subtraction, not assembly.

list: Print it, and keep a second copy on your phone. Tick each line as you make it.
Say the next group's names out loud before you finish the current one, so the helper is already moving.
If someone on the list is missing, note it with the time. 'She had left by 4:10' is an answer; 'I don't know' is not.

title: Late invoice reminder emails for photographers: three templates
description: Three short, non-awkward reminders for an unpaid photography invoice: before it is due, the day after, and two weeks late with your late-fee line.
intro: Most brand and editorial invoices are paid late by accounts-payable departments that are not ignoring you, they are batching. The trick is to be in the batch. These three notes are short enough to send without dread. Replace the brackets and keep your own sign-off.

sections.pre:
Subject: Invoice [number] for [project], due [date]

Hi [name],

Quick note that invoice [number] for [project] is due on [date]. If it is already in your run, ignore this. If anything is missing on my end for processing (PO number, vendor form, W-9), tell me and I will send it today.

Thanks,
[your name]

sections.h: 2. The day after due (plain and specific)
sections.pre:
Subject: Invoice [number] is now past due

Hi [name],

Invoice [number] for [amount] was due yesterday, [date]. Could you let me know when it is scheduled for payment? If it has been paid and is in transit, a remittance date is all I need.

Best,
[your name]

sections.h: 3. Two weeks late (firm, with your terms)
sections.pre:
Subject: Invoice [number], 14 days overdue

Hi [name],

Invoice [number] for [amount] is now 14 days past its due date of [date]. Per the terms on the invoice, a late fee of [fee or percentage] applies from [date]; I have attached an updated copy. Please confirm a payment date by [day], or let me know who else I should be speaking to.

Regards,
[your name]

list: Send them from the same thread as the original invoice so the history is one click away.
Name a date in every message. 'Soon' gives them nothing to put in a system.
Ask who else to contact. Accounts payable often sits with a different person than your creative contact.
Stop the sequence the moment money lands, and say thank you. Clients remember how the end felt.
Only mention a late fee if it is on the invoice they already accepted.

title: What to put in a photography pricing guide: a checklist
description: The sections a pricing guide needs so clients stop emailing questions, the order that sells the middle package, and the mistakes that make guides go stale.
intro: A pricing guide is a sales document that happens to contain prices. Most leak bookings because they answer the wrong questions, or because three versions are floating around. Here is a checklist for the content, then for keeping it current.

list: One paragraph on who you are for and what the experience is like. Not a biography.
Packages, three at most, with the middle one holding the things most people actually want. Name them by outcome, not by hours.
What is included in every package, written once, so the package table stays short.
Add-ons with prices: second shooter, extra hour, albums, prints, travel beyond a radius, rush delivery.
How booking works: retainer amount, when the balance is due, how to hold a date.
Turnaround, gallery window, and what happens if it rains or someone is ill.
Three answers to the questions you get every single time. Pull them from your actual inbox.
How to take the next step, one way only: a link to a call or an inquiry form.
A dated PDF. The moment prices change, every copy you ever sent becomes a quote you did not make. Keep one live link and let it update.
Hours as the headline. Clients do not know what eight hours of a wedding feels like. Lead with coverage of the moments.
Hiding the price range until the call. It filters out the wrong people only after they have cost you an hour.
Six packages. Choice overload reads as indecision. Three, with the middle one designed to win.
No expiry. State the guide's valid-until date so a 2024 version cannot be used in 2026.

p: Put the prices in one place you control and generate the guide from that, whether that is a spreadsheet and a template or a tool. Changing a price should be one edit, not a hunt through Dropbox.
Each time you send the guide, log who and when. Twice a year, email the people who received an old version and have not booked; a new version is a legitimate reason to reach out.

title: Do I need a permit to shoot here? A checklist for outdoor sessions
description: How to find the permit rule for a park, beach or street before you book a client there, what to ask the issuing office, and what to tell the client.
intro: Permit rules differ park by park, not city by city, and the fine or the eviction usually lands mid-session. This is the checklist to run before you confirm a location with a client. It is not legal advice; it is where to look and what to ask.

list: City parks: the city's parks and recreation department. Search the park name plus 'photography permit' and the department's own site, not a forum.
County and state parks: the park's own page usually has a 'commercial photography' or 'special use' section with a fee and a lead time.
Botanic gardens, arboretums, historic houses: almost always a permit, often with a per-session fee and limited slots. Book early in autumn.
Beaches and waterfronts: may be city, county, state or a port authority. The lifeguard tower sign often names the agency.
Streets and plazas: usually fine for a small crew without equipment on the ground; tripods, lights and blocking the pavement change the answer. Private plazas that look public are private.
Does a single photographer with one client and no lights or tripod need a permit, or only crews?
What is the fee, and is it per session, per day or annual?
How many days' notice, and is there a form or an email?
Are there blackout dates, closed areas or hours when permits are not issued?
Does the permit need insurance, and what minimum?
Can the permit be transferred to a backup date if it rains?

p: Put the permit status and fee in the booking notes and the invoice. If the location needs one, say who pays and that the date depends on approval. If it does not need one, say that too, so there is no surprise if a ranger asks.

Every time you check a location, record the rule, fee, lead time, link and the date you checked. In two seasons you will have the only accurate permit list for your city, and you will stop re-checking the same park every spring.

title: Gallery expiry reminder emails: three templates with an extension offer
description: Short reminders at 30, 7 and 1 days before a client gallery closes, written to get downloads, with a paid extension in the last one so the 'can you resend?' email never arrives.
intro: Clients do not forget to download because they do not care. They forget because the gallery email arrived in a busy week. Three reminders, each with the download count if your host shows it, turn a resend request into a download or a small extension sale.

sections.pre:
Subject: Your gallery closes on [date]

Hi [names],

A gentle note that your gallery stays open until [date]. If you have not downloaded the full set yet, now is a good time: [link]. The download button is top right, and the files are full resolution.

[your name]

Subject: One week left on your gallery

Hi [names],

Your gallery closes in a week, on [date]. I can see the full set has not been downloaded yet, so here is the link again: [link]. If you want it to stay open longer, a one-year extension is [price] and I can set it up in a minute.

[your name]

Subject: Last day for your gallery

Hi [names],

Your gallery closes tomorrow, [date]. Download the full set here: [link]. If you would rather keep it online, reply 'extend' and I will send a [price] link for another year, or [price] for a permanent archive.

Thank you again for having me,
[your name]

list: If your host shows download status, skip reminders for clients who already downloaded. A reminder to someone who has the files reads as noise.
Price the extension so it is a small yes, not a decision. Many photographers use the cost of a print or two.
Say what happens after expiry in plain words. 'Archived offline, retrievable for a fee' is honest; 'deleted' should only be said if it is true.
Keep every reminder in the same thread as the delivery email.

title: Second shooter call sheet template for weddings
description: A one-page call sheet for second shooters and assistants: times, locations, roles, shot list, gear, rate and payment, so nothing is agreed only in a text thread.
intro: A second shooter who shows up with the right lens at the right door is the result of one page sent the week before, not a text at midnight. Copy this and fill it in for every job.

sections.pre:
JOB: [couple's names], [date]
LEAD: [your name], [phone]
SECOND: [name], [phone]

CALL TIME: [time] at [address or pin]
WRAP: [time, or 'after first dance']

TIMELINE (second's role in brackets)
[time]  Getting ready, Partner B's suite  [cover Partner B; details, flat lays]
[time]  First look / ceremony arrivals    [guests arriving, wide of venue]
[time]  Ceremony                           [opposite angle to lead; reactions, back rows]
[time]  Family formals                     [gather next group from the list; grab candids]
[time]  Couple portraits                   [reception room empty, details, cocktail hour candids]
[time]  Reception                          [reactions during speeches; second angle on first dance]

MUST-HAVES FOR THE SECOND
- [e.g. grandmother arriving, groom's reaction, the band]

GEAR
Bring: [bodies, lenses, flash]. Cards: shoot to two cards, do not format. Hand over all cards at wrap.

FILES
Deliver: [raw cards / card copy / upload link] by [date]. No sharing or posting of any image; credit terms: [e.g. may share after the couple's gallery goes live, with credit to lead].

RATE AND PAYMENT
[amount] for [hours], overtime [rate]. Paid by [method] within [days] of delivery. Travel: [included / per mile].

DRESS: [dark, no logos]. PARKING: [note]. MEALS: [vendor meal confirmed / bring your own].

list: The approved family formals list, so they can gather the next group while you shoot.
A pin for every location, not just an address. Venues have the wrong front door.
Your phone number and the planner's, with a note on which one to call for what.
Confirm the cards or files arrived the same day, in writing.
Pay on the day you said. Reliability is why the good ones answer your next message first.
Keep a note of who was free, who was great and what they charged. Next season's list builds itself.

title: Corporate headshot day checklist: what to send HR before you arrive
description: A planning checklist for on-site company headshot days: slot maths, the email HR forwards to staff, the room you need, the on-the-day flow, and how picks and delivery stay out of your inbox.
intro: Headshot days are won or lost before the first frame: the right room, the right slot length, and one clear email to staff. This is the checklist I run with the HR contact two weeks out. Copy it into your own booking confirmation.

sections.h: Two weeks out: agree these with HR
list: Headcount, and whether leadership gets longer slots or a second look.
Slot length: ten minutes a person for a standard look with a quick review, fifteen if they pick their frame on the spot. Add a ten-minute buffer every hour.
The room: at least four metres long, blinds or no windows, a power socket, and no through traffic. A boardroom beats a lobby.
Look: background colour, framing (head and shoulders or waist up), dress note, and whether glasses stay on.
Who owns the schedule: you send a booking link, or HR fills a sheet. Decide now; both at once ends in double bookings.
Delivery: who picks the final frame, what retouching is included, file sizes, naming convention (firstname-lastname), and the deadline.
Invoice terms and any purchase order number, so payment does not wait on paperwork after the fact.

sections.h: The email HR forwards to staff (copy this)
sections.pre:
Subject: Headshots on [date], book your 10-minute slot

Hi all,

[Photographer] is in the office on [date] from [start] to [end] for new headshots. Book a slot here: [link]. It takes about ten minutes.

Wear what you would wear to meet a client; solid colours photograph best, and avoid fine stripes or large logos. Glasses are fine. Please arrive two minutes early.

You will get a link to choose your favourite frame within [n] days of the session.

[HR name]

list: Confirm the room is still yours and the slots are full; send the roster to HR with gaps marked so they can fill them.
Charge everything, pack a backup body, and bring a small mirror and a lint roller for the table by the door.
Print the roster. Phones die; paper does not.
Set up thirty minutes early and shoot a test frame of the HR contact; it checks the look and gives them a photo to send round as a nudge.
Tick people off as they arrive; anyone who misses their slot goes to a short waitlist at the end rather than being squeezed in.
Say the same three directions to everyone, in the same order. Consistency across eighty people is the product.
Before packing up, give HR a count: shot, no-shows, and who still needs a session.
Send pick links within the promised window, one per person, with a deadline. Unchosen picks after the deadline default to your choice; say so up front.
Deliver in one named folder to HR, plus the roster with status per person: picked, retouched, delivered.
Ask HR for the dates of their next intake. Headshot days recur; the second booking should be a reply, not a pitch.

title: Mini session day planning checklist: slots, deposits, waitlist, rain plan
description: How to plan a holiday or fall mini-session day so it fills, holds and runs on time: slot maths, deposit rules, the waitlist, what to send families, and the rain plan written before you need it.
intro: Mini days make or lose money in the planning week, not on the day. This is the checklist I use before announcing one. Copy it into your own notes and fill it in once; most of it carries over to the next date.

list: Date, location, and a backup date at the same location, booked now, not after the forecast turns.
Slot length and count: fifteen minutes with a five-minute buffer gives three families an hour; twelve slots is a full afternoon of light in autumn.
Price, deposit and what is included: say the image count and the delivery window in the first message, not the third.
Deposit rule in one sentence: holds the slot, applied to the balance, moved to the backup date for weather, refunded only if you cancel.
Cut-off: when booking closes and when the balance is due, so the day before is not a payment chase.
One page or post with the slots visible. Families book faster when they can see which times are left.
Take the deposit at booking; a slot without money is a maybe. Maybes are what no-shows are made of.

Open a waitlist the moment the last slot goes. A cancellation offered to the next name on the list is filled within the hour; a cancellation announced publicly is filled by someone you have to onboard from scratch.
Announce once, remind twice: a week out and two days out, with the forecast and the rain plan in the second.

sections.h: What each family gets after booking
sections.pre:
Subject: Your mini session: [date], [time]

Hi [name],

You are booked for [time] on [date] at [location]: [pin or link]. Please arrive ten minutes early; we start on the minute so every family gets their full slot.

What to wear: [two lines, your palette]. What to bring: [props, snacks, a change of clothes for toddlers].

Rain plan: if the forecast on the morning shows [your rule, e.g. more than 60 percent chance of rain at your time], we move to [backup date] at the same time and your deposit moves with you. I will message by [time] that morning.

Gallery: [n] images within [n] days, with a link to choose extras.

[your name]

list: Arrive an hour early, walk the light, choose two spots so a crying toddler can be moved, not stopped.
Keep a printed list by time with phone numbers. Tick as families arrive; text the next family when you are running five minutes behind so they do not stack up.
Shoot the first frame on the minute. Fifteen minutes is enough when you are not spending five of them deciding where to stand.
Hold the last slot for the waitlist no-show rule: if a family is ten minutes late with no message, text the next waitlisted family for the final slot.
Deliver on the day you promised, all galleries at once, with the extras link live.
Before galleries go out, send the next date to this list first. A family that just loved their photos books the spring minis in the same message.
Write down what broke: the slot that ran long, the spot that lost light, the deposit question you answered six times. Fix the page, not your memory.

title: How to stop snacking after dinner: a plan for the evening
description: A plain plan for the hours after dinner: set a kitchen-closed time, plan the snack you will have, change what the evening looks like, and get through a craving without relying on willpower.
intro: If you eat well all day and then lose it after 8pm, the problem is usually the evening, not your willpower. The hours after dinner come with tiredness, boredom, a screen and an open kitchen. This plan changes the evening so there is less to resist.

sections.h: Decide the rule before the evening starts
list: Pick a kitchen-closed time, for example 30 to 60 minutes after dinner. Write it down. A rule you set at noon is easier to keep than a decision you make at 9pm.
Plan one evening snack if you want one, and decide what it is in advance. A planned snack is part of the day; an unplanned one is the slide.
Make the rule about time, not food. "Nothing after 8:30 except tea" is easier to follow than a list of banned foods.

sections.h: Change the setting, not just the snack
list: Eat enough at dinner, including protein and vegetables. A light or skipped dinner makes the late-evening hunger real.
Close the kitchen visibly: lights off, dishes done, and snacks put out of sight or not bought at all.
Brush your teeth soon after the cutoff. Many people find it ends the eating part of the day.
Notice the trigger. If it starts with a show, a drink, or a partner opening the snacks, plan for that moment specifically.
Wait ten minutes before deciding. Set a timer. Cravings usually rise and then fade within minutes.
While you wait, drink a glass of water or tea, step out of the kitchen, or do something with your hands.
After the timer, decide again. If you still want the planned snack, have it and enjoy it. The goal is a choice, not a ban.
Track one thing: did I keep my evening rule tonight? Yes or no.
Count the streak, but a missed night is one night. Start again the next evening without making up for it.
Look at the misses after a week. They usually share a cause, such as late meetings, a skipped lunch or a certain show, and that cause is what to fix.

p: This is a habit plan for everyday evening snacking. If eating often feels out of control, comes with distress, or you are worried about your weight or health, talk to a doctor or a registered dietitian.
